description: Monopoly and oligopoly, barriers to entry, and the advantages and drawbacks of market power for consumers.
content_html:
When Markets Lose Competition

In a non-competitive market, competition is weak or absent. Instead of dozens of firms all trying to undercut each other, one firm — or a handful — dominates the whole market. This changes everything for consumers: prices tend to rise, choice narrows, and the pressure to innovate or cut costs disappears. Understanding non-competitive markets matters because they are everywhere in the real world, from your broadband provider to the operating system on your phone.

Economists distinguish market structures partly by asking: how many sellers are there, how similar are the products, and how easy is it for a new firm to enter? In a competitive market, entry is easy and no single firm can dictate price. Move along the spectrum and you reach monopoly at one extreme — a single dominant supplier with enormous market power.

Key Fact

For the purposes of GCSE Economics, a firm is said to have monopoly power if it holds 25% or more of market supply — this is the share-of-supply threshold used in merger control under the Enterprise Act 2002. A firm with 100% of the market is a pure monopoly, but even a firm with a large share can exercise significant monopoly power. The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) investigates firms suspected of abusing that power.

Barriers to Entry: The Wall That Keeps Rivals Out

Monopoly power is sustained by barriers to entry. Without these barriers, high profits would attract new competitors, eroding the dominant firm’s advantage. The main barriers are:

High start-up costs. Building a national railway network, laying undersea cables or constructing a semiconductor factory costs billions of pounds. Few new entrants can raise this capital, so existing firms are protected by sheer scale.

Economies of scale. A dominant firm producing millions of units has much lower average costs than a new entrant producing a few thousand. The new entrant cannot price competitively until it reaches the same scale — but it cannot grow until it attracts customers away from the cheaper incumbent. This is a catch-22 that keeps many rivals out.

Patents and legal protection. Pharmaceutical companies hold patents giving them the exclusive right to produce a drug for around 20 years. During that window, the patent-holder is the only legal supplier and can charge a high price. Once the patent expires, generic manufacturers enter and prices fall sharply.

Brand loyalty and switching costs. Customers who are deeply familiar with a product, or who would face cost and inconvenience in switching, are ‘locked in’ even if a rival offers a better deal. A student who has used the same cloud storage service for years may stay even if a cheaper alternative exists, simply because transferring files is tedious.

How a Monopolist Behaves: Price Maker, Not Price Taker

In a competitive market every firm is a price taker: it accepts the market price and cannot charge more without losing all customers to identical rivals. A monopolist faces no such constraint. It is a price maker — it sets its own price by choosing how much output to produce. To sell more, it lowers its price; to push the price up, it restricts supply. This is the core of monopoly power.

Imagine a single internet provider in a rural area where no other network reaches. Residents must either pay the provider’s price or go without broadband. The provider has no incentive to cut prices, improve service or invest in the fastest technology unless a rival threatens to enter its market. Without competition, consumer welfare suffers.

Not every consequence of monopoly is negative. A large firm that dominates its market can benefit from significant economies of scale, driving its average costs down. If it passes some of those savings to consumers through lower prices, the outcome may be better than having many small, high-cost rivals.

Large dominant firms also tend to invest more heavily in research and development (R&D). A pharmaceutical giant earning high profits on patented drugs can afford to spend billions searching for new treatments. A small competitive firm operating on thin margins may not have the resources to fund the same level of innovation. This argument is often used to defend the patent system: the promise of temporary monopoly profits incentivises the risky, expensive work of discovering new medicines and technologies.

There are also cases where having a single large supplier is simply more efficient — these are called natural monopolies. Laying duplicate water pipes or electricity cables to every home would be wasteful. In such industries, one network provider is cheaper than two or three, so regulation rather than competition is the preferred solution.

Oligopoly: Competition Between the Few

Most real markets sit between perfect competition and pure monopoly. Oligopoly is the most common non-competitive structure in advanced economies. Think of the UK supermarket sector, where a handful of large chains — including Tesco, Sainsbury’s, Asda, Aldi and Morrisons — account for the majority of grocery sales. By 2025, Aldi had overtaken Morrisons to become the fourth-largest grocer by market share, reflecting how discounters have disrupted the traditional market. Or consider the UK mobile network market, where a small number of providers share the vast majority of customers.

The defining feature of oligopoly is interdependence: each firm’s decisions about price, output and advertising are influenced by what it expects its rivals to do. If one supermarket cuts prices on bread, the others must decide whether to match the cut or risk losing customers. This makes oligopoly markets dynamic and sometimes unpredictable.

Oligopolists face a choice. They can compete fiercely — cutting prices, ramping up advertising, launching new products — which pushes prices down and benefits consumers but squeezes their own profits. This is a price war, and it can be damaging for all firms involved.

Alternatively, they can act together. Collusion occurs when rival firms co-ordinate their behaviour rather than competing. In its most obvious form, they meet secretly to fix prices — this is called a cartel. Cartels are illegal under UK competition law (Competition Act 1998, enforced by the CMA) because they eliminate competition and harm consumers through artificially high prices.

Collusion can also be tacit: firms follow the price leader without any formal agreement. If one airline raises its prices and rivals quietly follow suit, prices settle at a higher level without a single phone call being made. Tacit collusion is harder to prosecute but has the same effect — consumers pay more.

The Impact on Consumers and Workers

The clearest cost of non-competitive markets falls on consumers. A price maker charges more than a price taker would. Because the monopolist or oligopolist faces limited competitive pressure, it also has less reason to improve quality, reduce waiting times or invest in customer service. Choice is restricted — consumers cannot easily find an equivalent alternative. In the most extreme cases, consumers must accept whatever the single supplier provides or go without.

Workers are also affected. In highly competitive labour markets, firms bid up wages to attract staff. A firm with substantial market power, however, can sometimes extend that power into the labour market, suppressing wages — a situation economists call monopsony power in the labour market. Conversely, the higher profits earned by dominant firms can sometimes fund better pay and conditions for their own employees.

Key Fact

Monopoly and oligopoly typically lead to higher prices, less choice, and lower quality for consumers compared with competitive markets. However, large dominant firms may invest more in R&D, achieve greater economies of scale, and in natural-monopoly industries a single supplier can be more efficient than many competing networks.

Government Regulation of Monopoly Power

Because of the harm non-competitive markets can cause, governments intervene. The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) in the UK can investigate mergers that would create a dominant firm, break up companies if market power is being abused, and impose fines on firms found to be running cartels or engaging in anti-competitive behaviour. The CMA can also order a dominant firm to allow rivals access to its infrastructure — for example, requiring a dominant broadband network owner to let competing providers use its cables at a fair price.

In natural monopoly industries such as water and energy, the government uses price regulation to cap what companies can charge. A regulator sets a maximum price that the natural monopolist may charge, preventing it from exploiting consumers while still allowing it to earn enough to maintain and invest in its network.
exam_tip_html: The command word Analyse asks you to build a connected chain of cause and effect — not just list features. A strong answer traces the full logical path: for example, “barriers to entry prevent new firms competing → the monopolist faces no pressure to cut prices → consumers pay above the competitive price → consumer surplus falls.” For Evaluate questions about monopoly, the key is to present both the case against (higher prices, less choice, lower quality) and the case for (economies of scale, R&D investment, natural monopoly efficiency), then reach a supported judgement — for example, whether the harm outweighs the benefit depends on the industry type, the size of the barriers to entry, and whether regulation is effective. Avoid simply listing pros and cons and leaving the examiner to choose a winner.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A monopoly is a single dominant supplier with the power to set its own price; barriers to entry — such as high capital costs, economies of scale and patents — protect its position from new rivals.
  • An oligopoly is dominated by a small number of large firms; their interdependence means rivalry can lead to price wars or, illegally, to collusion that raises prices above the competitive level.
  • Non-competitive markets generally harm consumers through higher prices and less choice, but can deliver benefits such as economies of scale and R&D investment; the government uses the CMA and price regulation to limit abuse of market power.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a barrier to entry that protects a monopolist's position?
A) Low start-up costs
B) Many rival firms in the market
C) A patent giving exclusive rights to produce a product
D) A price below the competitive level
practice_questions.marks: C) A patent giving exclusive rights to produce a product. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
A firm produces 50,000 units and sells them at £8 each. Its total costs are £320,000.

Calculate the firm's profit.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for the correct method: Profit = Total Revenue − Total Costs; Total Revenue = 50,000 × £8 = £400,000; Profit = £400,000 − £320,000.
1 mark for the correct answer of £80,000.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why a monopolist is able to charge a higher price than a firm in a competitive market.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for identifying a relevant reason, for example: a monopolist faces no close competition / faces no substitute products / has significant barriers to entry protecting its market.
1 mark for developing the point: because there are no rival firms able to offer the same product, consumers have no alternative supplier to turn to.
1 mark for a further development: this means the monopolist can restrict output and raise its price without losing all its customers, unlike a price taker who would lose all sales to rivals if it charged above the market price.

practice_questions.text:
GigaStream is the only broadband provider in a rural region. It has very high average costs compared with large urban providers and charges customers significantly more than the national average.

Explain, using the concept of barriers to entry, why GigaStream is able to maintain its dominant position in this market.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for identifying a relevant barrier, for example: the high cost of laying cable infrastructure / the need for significant capital investment before any revenue is earned.
1 mark for developing how this creates a barrier: a new entrant would need to invest very large sums in a second network before attracting a single customer, making entry financially risky.
1 mark for a further development linked to economies of scale: GigaStream, even though small, is the only provider in the region — a new entrant would be even smaller and face even higher average costs per customer, making it impossible to undercut GigaStream's price and still cover costs.
1 mark for linking back to market power: because no rival can profitably enter, GigaStream retains its position as the only supplier and can continue charging above-competitive prices.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how an oligopoly in the UK supermarket sector affects consumers.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A detailed, connected chain of reasoning showing how the small number of dominant firms creates interdependence, explaining the possible consequences (price wars benefiting consumers, or tacit collusion harming them), with both the positive and negative effects on consumers clearly analysed and a developed explanation of at least one mechanism (e.g. tacit collusion → prices settle above competitive level → consumer surplus reduced).
Secure (3–4 marks): Clear analysis of at least one route by which oligopoly affects consumers, with a developed chain of reasoning. May lack full development of both sides or the interdependence mechanism.
Developing (1–2 marks): Some relevant points about oligopoly or consumer impact, but limited connection between them. May list features without explaining the chain of causation.
Emerging (0 marks): No creditworthy content.

practice_questions.text:
'A monopoly always harms the economy and should always be broken up by the government.'

Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support (monopoly harms economy):
• A monopolist is a price maker and faces no competitive pressure to reduce prices — consumers pay above the competitive price, reducing consumer welfare.
• With no rivals, the monopolist has little incentive to improve quality, innovate or invest in better customer service, leading to productive and dynamic inefficiency.
• High barriers to entry prevent new firms from bringing fresh competition, locking in the dominant firm's position indefinitely.
• Workers in monopsonistic labour markets may face suppressed wages, worsening inequality.

Arguments against (monopoly may not always harm):
• A dominant firm can achieve significant economies of scale, lowering average costs; if some savings are passed to consumers through lower prices, consumers may be better off than with many small high-cost rivals.
• Large firms earning high profits can invest heavily in R&D, potentially generating innovations that benefit the wider economy — the pharmaceutical industry is often cited as an example.
• Natural monopolies (water, electricity networks) are more efficient as a single network — breaking them up would lead to costly duplication of infrastructure and higher, not lower, average costs.
• Government regulation (CMA price caps, access requirements) can control the worst excesses of monopoly power without the disruption of a forced break-up.

Judgement: The appropriate response depends on the type of monopoly, the size of the efficiency gains, and the effectiveness of regulation. In natural-monopoly industries, regulation rather than break-up is likely to be better for consumers. In markets where barriers to entry are artificial (e.g. a firm that has acquired rivals simply to eliminate competition), a break-up or prohibition of the merger is more justified. A blanket rule that all monopolies should always be broken up ignores these important differences.

Mastering (10–12 marks): Sophisticated evaluation of both sides with specific examples, a reasoned judgement that uses ‘it depends on’ language and identifies the key condition(s) that determine the outcome. Sustained, well-structured argument throughout.
Secure (7–9 marks): Clear argument with relevant evidence on both sides and an attempt at a supported judgement. Some analysis may lack full development.
Developing (4–6 marks): Points made on both sides but explanation is limited; judgement may be present but unsupported.
Emerging (1–3 marks): Simple points, largely one-sided; little or no judgement.

knowledge_checks.q: Which market structure is dominated by a small number of large firms that are mutually aware of each other's actions?
Which of the following best describes a barrier to entry?
options: A government subsidy paid to new firms entering a market
An obstacle that makes it difficult or costly for new firms to compete with existing ones
The price charged by the dominant firm in the market
The number of workers employed in a competitive industry

knowledge_checks.q: A monopolist is described as a price _____ because it can set its own price by controlling how much output it produces.
When rival firms secretly agree to fix prices or share markets, this is known as _____.
Match each term to its correct description:
right: An obstacle preventing new firms from entering a market
A market dominated by a small number of large, interdependent firms
An industry where a single supplier is more efficient than several competing networks

flashcard_questions.a: A market where one or a few large firms dominate, giving them significant power over price.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a barrier to entry?
flashcard_questions.a: An obstacle making it difficult or costly for new firms to enter and compete in a market.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one example of a barrier to entry based on legal protection.
flashcard_questions.a: A patent granting a firm exclusive rights to produce a product for around 20 years.

flashcard_questions.q: In a competitive market a firm is a price taker. What is a monopolist instead?
flashcard_questions.a: A price maker — it sets its own price by choosing how much output to produce.
A market dominated by a small number of large firms, each aware of its rivals' actions.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the key feature that makes oligopoly markets different from competitive markets?
flashcard_questions.a: Interdependence — each firm's decisions are shaped by what it expects rivals to do.

flashcard_questions.q: What is collusion in an oligopoly?
flashcard_questions.a: An agreement between rival firms to fix prices or share markets, raising profits above the competitive level.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is collusion illegal under UK competition law (Competition Act 1998)?
flashcard_questions.a: Because it eliminates competition and harms consumers through artificially high prices; the CMA investigates and fines firms involved.

flashcard_questions.q: State one advantage of a monopoly for the economy.
flashcard_questions.a: Economies of scale lower average costs, and high profits can fund greater R&D investment.
An industry where a single supplier is more efficient than several competing networks (e.g. water pipes).

flashcard_questions.q: Which UK government body investigates firms suspected of abusing market dominance?
How does a monopolist restrict supply to raise its price?
flashcard_questions.a: By producing less output than a competitive market would, pushing the market price above the competitive level.

flashcard_questions.q: State one way the government can regulate a natural monopoly without breaking it up.
flashcard_questions.a: By setting a maximum price (price cap) the firm may charge consumers.

glossary_terms.definition: A market in which one or a small number of large firms dominate, giving them significant power over price and output.
A market structure in which one firm supplies the entire market and faces no close competition.
The ability of a firm to influence the price it charges for its product, because it faces little or no competition.
Obstacles that make it difficult or costly for new firms to enter a market and compete with existing firms.
A market structure dominated by a small number of large firms, each of which is aware of the actions of its rivals.
An agreement between competing firms to fix prices, share markets or restrict output in order to raise profits above the competitive level.
